Figure caption: Endocytic and nonendocytic pathways of cellular internalization. Schematic representation of major endocytic and nonendocytic entry pathways. Endocytic pathways are subdivided into pinocytosis and phagocytosis. Arf6 regulates postendocytic recycling rather than initial uptake. Nonendocytic pathways include direct membrane fusion, pore formation, and membrane penetration. Solid black arrows indicate predominant trafficking routes, whereas dashed arrows indicate alternative routes occasionally observed. Early endosomal convergence is common for all pathways, with subsequent trafficking to late endosomes and lysosomes or detours via recycling endosomes or the ER/Golgi network.

Figure caption: Schematic representation of endosomal maturation. PM-derived endocytic vesicles fuse with early endosomes, enriched in phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate [PI(3)­P] (green), and serve as the primary sorting station for internalized cargo, a process that typically occurs within minutes of uptake. Cargo can undergo fast recycling directly to the PM or be routed to recycling endosomes, enriched in phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate [PI(4)­P] (red), for slow recycling. Maturation into late endosomes/multivesicular bodies (MVBs), which occurs over tens of minutes, is characterized by Rab5 to Rab7 conversion, enrichment of BMP/LBPA (blue), formation of intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) via the ESCRT machinery, and progressive acidification through V-ATPase activity. Late endosomes can fuse with lysosomes to form endolysosomes or with autophagosomes to generate amphisomes and subsequently merge with lysosomes to produce autolysosomes (depicted at reduced opacity to emphasize the primary maturation pathway). Exosomal secretion occurs upon fusion of MVBs with the PM (legend: Rab; Ras-associated binding, EEA; Early endosome antigen, LC3; Microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3, LAMP; Lysosome-associated membrane glycoproteins, ATP; Adenosine triphosphate, ESCRT; Endosomal sorting complex required for transport, MVB; Multivesicular body).

Figure caption: Pathogen-derived mechanisms of endosomal escape. Representative strategies of endosomal escape by natural pathogenic systems, which occur over time scales ranging from minutes to over an hour depending on the pathogen and host cell. Membrane fusion: Zika virus uses its envelope protein to fuse with the endosomal membrane under acidic conditions, releasing the capsid into the cytosol, where it subsequently disassembles to release the viral genome. Pore formation: Listeria monocytogenes secretes listeriolysin O (LLO) and phospholipases, which together disrupt the endosomal membrane. LLO oligomerizes into pores in response to acidification and reductive activation by gamma-interferon-inducible lysosomal thiol (GILT) reductase, while phospholipases hydrolyze host phospholipids, enabling bacterial escape. Membrane destabilization: Adenovirus capsids undergo disassembly in acidic compartments, exposing protein VI that induces positive curvature and destabilizes the endosomal membrane, resulting in rupture and genome release. Endogenous stimuli-triggered escape: Ebola virus requires sequential host cues to facilitate fusion; endosomal cathepsins cleave the glycan cap of its glycoprotein, thereby exposing the NPC1 receptor-binding site, and engagement with NPC1 enables subsequent membrane fusion and genome release. Collectively, these pathogen-derived strategies exemplify diverse solutions for breaching endosomal membranes and provide a blueprint for designing synthetic delivery systems.

Figure caption: Engineered strategies for endosomal escape. Overview of synthetic approaches to facilitate cytosolic delivery. Carrier engineering: Structural modifications of delivery vehicles, including lipid nanoparticles that undergo membrane destabilization and fusion, release cargo into the cytosol. EV-inspired: Vesicle inspired systems incorporating EV components, such as surface proteins or fusogenic peptides, to enhance membrane fusion and cargo delivery. Stimuli-responsive: Platforms responding to endogenous cues or exogenous triggers, such as pH-responsive nanogels that undergo protonation and swelling, rupturing the endosomal membrane. Biomimetic: Pathogen-inspired approaches utilizing viral fusogenic peptides or cell-penetrating peptides to achieve direct membrane penetration or fusion. Inherent properties: Cationic polymers exploit intrinsic physicochemical properties, such as buffering capacity, to drive chloride influx, osmotic swelling, and membrane rupture. Hybrid and multifunctional platforms: Synergistic integration of multiple mechanisms within a single delivery system to enhance escape efficiency.
